The Spoon River Clarion's printing press was destroyed, and I suffered the punishment of being tarred and feathered. My offense was publishing the following piece on the very day the Anarchists met their execution by hanging in Chicago:

"A blindfolded woman of great beauty stood atop the steps of a temple carved from marble. Countless people streamed past her, their faces raised in desperate appeal. Clutched in her left hand was a sword, which she swung without pattern—striking down a child one moment, a worker the next, then a cowering woman, then someone unhinged by madness. Her right hand held a set of scales, into which those escaping the sword's blows would throw coins of gold.

A figure clothed in black robes recited from a scroll: 'She shows no favoritism among people.'

Suddenly a young man in a crimson cap rushed forward and tore the blindfold from her face. What lay beneath was horrifying—the eyelashes had rotted away entirely, leaving raw and weeping lids; her eyes themselves were clouded with a thick, milky film; her expression bore the unmistakable mark of a soul consumed by madness as it perished.

Only then did the crowd comprehend the true purpose behind her blindfold."

# The Press of the Spoon River Clarion

They came in the night, as such men always do, and destroyed my press—the very instrument through which I had dared to speak truth to this town. The type was scattered into the mud, the platen smashed beyond repair, and the building itself set alight before dawn could reveal their faces. This was their answer to what I had printed, their retaliation swift and merciless, as if silencing the machine could silence the truth it had given voice to.

I had published my piece on the day the Chicago Anarchists were hanged—that day when the state chose to answer ideas with rope, when men were executed not for what they had done but for what they had dared to believe. It seemed to me the fitting moment to speak of justice, of what she truly was beneath her marble countenance, and so I wrote of a vision that had come to me, a vision I could not keep silent.

In this vision I saw a woman, blindfolded, robed in the ancient trappings of her office, moving through a crowd with a sword in one hand and a scale in the other. She struck as she pleased—the innocent alongside the guilty, the humble alongside the proud—while all the while her scale filled steadily with gold, coin upon coin dropping into its pan as if payment were the only true measure she recognized. She did not pause to weigh mercy or truth; she only struck, and collected, and struck again.

Beside her stood a man in a black gown, solemn as any judge, who lifted his voice to the gathered crowd and declared her sacred impartiality: "Behold," he said, "she is no respecter of persons." And the crowd, hearing this, nodded in solemn agreement, believing perhaps that blindness itself was the very guarantee of fairness, that what she could not see, she could not favor.

But then a youth—bold, or perhaps merely reckless with the clarity of youth—stepped forward from the crowd and tore the blindfold from her eyes.

What was revealed was horror. Her eyes were not merely sightless but diseased, clouded with a milky corruption, glinting with the light of madness. She was not impartial because she was blind to favoritism—she was blind because disease had eaten through whatever vision she once possessed. The crowd recoiled as one, seeing at last what I had tried to tell them in print: that the justice they trusted, the justice that struck down anarchists and radicals alike while gold piled ever higher in her scale, was no true justice at all. She was corruption wearing the mask of impartiality, madness dressed in the robes of law.

For this vision, for daring to print such things on the very day when the state hanged men for their beliefs, they came for me. They dragged me from my bed, stripped me, and covered me in tar and feathers, parading me through the streets I had once walked freely. And when that humiliation was not enough, they returned to finish what they had started—they destroyed my press, as if by silencing the instrument of my voice, they might also silence the vision I had seen, and the truth that vision had dared to reveal.

# The Blind Goddess

I had built the *Clarion* with my own hands—every subscriber won by argument, every advertiser courted with patience, every line of type set with the conviction that a free press was worth more than the comfort of silence. For six years it had served this town honestly, and I had never known what it meant to fear my own words until the week the state of Illinois hanged four men for a crime that half the nation suspected they had not committed.

It was November of 1887, and the city was still raw from the executions. I had watched the papers fill with self-congratulation, with editorials praising the swift arm of the law, and I could not hold my tongue. I wrote a poem—an allegory, nothing more—and set it on the front page to run the very morning after the gallows had done their work.

I called her Justice, as she is always called. I gave her the sword, the scale, the blindfold that men have painted on her for centuries as proof of her impartiality. But in my verses she did not weigh evidence with trembling care; she swept her blade in wide, careless arcs, striking down whoever stood nearest, guilty or innocent alike, while into her outstretched palm—the one not gripping steel—men of wealth and influence pressed coins of gold, and her fingers closed around them with the ease of long practice. I meant it, I confess, as a judgment on the trial that had just ended: on a jury selected for its prejudice, on a judge who had all but pronounced sentence before the evidence was heard, on the newspapers that had convicted the accused in print months before the state did so in law.

I did not expect subtlety to save me, and it did not.

They came before dawn, a crowd of perhaps thirty men who called themselves patriots and who had, I later learned, been drinking since midnight to fortify themselves for the work ahead. They broke the press with sledgehammers—I heard the iron scream as the cylinders buckled—and they scattered the type until the floor of my shop looked like a beach of lead and steel. Then they took me.

I will not dwell long on what tar and feathers do to a man's skin, nor on the particular humiliation of being paraded through streets I had walked as a respected citizen only the day before. I remember the rail, and the jeers, and a boy—no older than twelve—running alongside the procession with a stick, prodding at me as though I were some captured animal too dangerous to touch with bare hands. I remember thinking, with the strange clarity that comes in extremity, that I had drawn Justice as blind and corrupt, and here was corruption enacting itself upon my own body in the light of morning, entirely unblinded, entirely willing to see exactly what it was doing.

But it is the boy I must tell you of, for he is the reason I write this at all rather than simply nursing my wounds in silence.

He was not part of the mob, or not truly—one of those boys who follow any commotion for the spectacle of it, indifferent to cause. Somewhere in the town square, where they had paused to let the crowd swell further before continuing my circuit, this boy had found a scrap of my ruined broadsheet, the very page bearing my poem, half-burned at its edges. And on that page was an illustration I had commissioned to accompany the verse: Justice with her bandage, her sword, her open palm. Children have a way of seeing what adults have trained themselves to overlook, and this boy—I do not know his name, and I have never learned it since—climbed onto the base of the courthouse statue, the real statue of Justice that stood in bronze above us all, and with a boy's mixture of mischief and something almost sacred, he reached up and tore the strip of cloth that decorative custom had draped across her sculpted eyes.

The crowd's noise faltered. I remember that falter more clearly than I remember my own pain.

For the eyes beneath that bandage—and here I must ask you to believe me, though I have turned the memory over a thousand times searching for some trick of light, some illusion born of my own suffering, and found none—the eyes were not merely sculpted blank, as such statues always are. They were clouded, discolored, weeping some dark rheum that had stained the bronze beneath in long streaks, as though the corrosion of decades had settled precisely there, at the one place custom had always kept covered. Justice was not impartial. Justice was diseased. Her blindness, which men had praised for a thousand years as the very guarantee of her fairness, was nothing but the visible symptom of a rot that had been eating her from within long before any of us were born to inherit her.

The crowd did not know what to do with this. A mob requires a kind of confidence to sustain its cruelty, and confidence cannot easily survive an omen. Men who a moment before had been howling for further indignities against me now stood staring upward at green-black streaks running down a stone face, murmuring to one another, crossing themselves, some of them already backing toward the edges of the square as though the statue's corruption might prove contagious.

I will not pretend that this vision saved me from further violence that day, nor that it produced any immediate reckoning with the men who had destroyed my press and my livelihood. The mob dispersed unevenly, its energy broken rather than redirected, and I was left to crawl home through back streets, avoiding the eyes of neighbors who did not know whether to pity me or condemn me further.

But something had been said that morning that could not be unsaid. I had written of a blind goddess who took bribes and struck without discernment, and thinking myself merely clever, merely bold, I had not imagined that the town itself would provide so literal and so damning an illustration of my metaphor—not from my pen, but from its own crumbling monuments, its own poisoned foundations, laid bare by a child's careless hand at the exact moment when the town most needed to believe in its own fairness.

I have rebuilt nothing since. The *Clarion* is ash and twisted metal, sold for scrap to pay what debts survived the fire that followed the initial destruction. I write this account now not to reclaim what was taken from me, but because I cannot stop seeing that bronze face, streaked and weeping, whenever I close my eyes—and because I suspect that what that boy uncovered was never mine to discover alone. It was always there, beneath the bandage we have all agreed, for centuries, not to remove.
outputs.L5:
# The Spoon River

The Spoon River is a modest waterway winding through the heart of Illinois, stretching approximately 148 miles before joining the Illinois River. Though unremarkable in size compared to America's great rivers, this humble tributary has secured a lasting place in American literary history, immortalized by poet Edgar Lee Masters in his groundbreaking work, "Spoon River Anthology," published in 1915.

Masters grew up in the small towns of Petersburg and Lewistown, Illinois, both situated along the Spoon River's banks. His intimate knowledge of these communities—their secrets, tragedies, hopes, and hypocrisies—became the foundation for one of American poetry's most innovative works. The anthology consists of free verse epitaphs spoken by the deceased residents of the fictional town of Spoon River, each revealing intimate truths about their lives that they could never share while living.

What makes the collection so powerful is its unflinching honesty. Masters gave voice to over 200 characters—farmers, lawyers, ministers, adulterers, drunkards, and dreamers—who speak from beyond the grave with a candor impossible in life. Themes of thwarted ambition, hidden scandal, quiet desperation, and occasional redemption weave through the collection, creating a mosaic portrait of small-town American life that challenged the sentimental pastoral ideals common in earlier literature.

The river itself, then, serves as more than mere setting; it symbolizes the flow of time and human experience, connecting generations of ordinary people whose individual stories, when woven together, create something universal. Masters transformed a small, geographically insignificant river into a powerful metaphor for mortality, memory, and the hidden complexity beneath the surface of seemingly simple lives.

Today, the actual Spoon River continues to flow quietly through Illinois farmland, largely unknown outside literary circles, while its poetic counterpart remains a testament to how art can elevate the local and specific into something that speaks to the universal human condition.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a Spoon River Anthology–style monologue from the perspective of a small-town newspaper editor who was punished for printing something controversial about the Haymarket executions?
counterfactuals.output:
**THEODORE FLINT**

I wrote that the men hanged in Chicago
were murdered by the state as surely as
the man who threw the bomb murdered in the Square—
not because I loved their creed,
which was smoke and fever to me,
but because a trial conducted in the newspapers
before it was conducted in the courts
is no trial at all, only a lynching with a docket number.

I printed this on a Thursday.
By Saturday the Commercial Club had met
in the back room of Riddle's grocery,
and my creditors remembered debts
they had forgotten for a decade.
The Baptist minister preached on the anarchist canker
without once saying my name,
which was worse than if he had.

By the following spring
my wife took the children to her sister's in Peoria,
and the subscribers fell away like leaves off the sycamore in front of the courthouse,
and Colonel Rutherford, who owned the bank
and most of the county besides,
bought my press at the sheriff's sale
for the value of the metal in it.

I sell insurance now, in the next county,
under my wife's maiden name.

And here I lie, Theodore Flint,
who was told that a free press
means the freedom to agree,
and who learned, a little too late for the learning to do him good,
that the town will forgive a drunkard,
a swindler, even a man who beats his wife—
but never a man who makes it think
when it would rather feel righteous.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Please compose a free-verse poem in the voice of a dead newspaper publisher explaining why his press was destroyed after printing an allegory about corrupt justice.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Fire Understood**

I set the type myself that night,
each letter cold and small as a tooth
pulled from the mouth of something honest.
The story was only a story—
a fox appointed judge over the henhouse,
a scale that tipped whichever way
the fox's own hunger leaned.
I called it *fable*. I called it *safe*.
I was wrong about the second word.

They came before the ink had dried enough
to stop smearing under thumbs.
I want to tell you it was about the press itself,
the great iron body of it,
the smell of oil and paper dust
that lived in my hair like a second scalp—
but iron is only iron.
What they hated was the mirror,
how the fox in my fable wore a collar
they recognized from their own closets,
how the henhouse had a name
if you turned the page sideways
and let the streetlight fall on it right.

Understand: allegory is a slow bullet.
It travels through the reader
long after the gun has been put down,
lodges somewhere behind the sternum,
and waits.
They could not un-know
what the story had shown them—
that justice, dressed in her blindfold,
had been peeking the whole time,
had seen exactly whose palm
held the coin, and smiled.

So they broke what could be broken.
Not the truth—you cannot break a truth
with an axe handle or a torch,
though God knows they tried that too.
They broke the *machine* that kept saying it,
the way you'd smash a bell
to stop it ringing the hour
you don't want anyone to know has come.

I watched from where I was already leaving,
the way you watch a house
you know you'll never sleep in again.
The type scattered like teeth across the floor—
o's and e's and the small hard consonants
of everything I still meant to say.

They thought silence was the same as innocence.
They thought if no one printed the fable,
the fox would forget he was a fox,
the hens would forget to count themselves
each morning and come up short.

But I am telling you now,
in whatever voice the dead are given,
that the story survived the burning
the way stories always do—
not in the paper, which was only ever paper,
but in the shape of what got broken,
which is its own kind of headline,
set in a type no fire has ever learned
to hold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about Lady Justice depicted with a bandage hiding diseased, blind eyes, revealed by a young radical, set against the backdrop of the 1887 Chicago Anarchist hangings.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Blindfold's Truth

In marble halls where justice stands,
her scales suspended in cold hands,
a bandage wraps her sightless face—
we called it balance, called it grace.

But in November's bitter chill,
eighty-seven, Chicago still
remembers rope and gallows-beam,
where Parsons, Spies, and Engel's dream
of bread and hours fairly won
was answered by the hangman's sun.

A boy stood watching, young and lean,
who'd seen what those in power mean
when they invoke her sacred name—
the bomb, the trial, the rush to blame,
the jury picked, the judge's hand
already writing the command
before the evidence was weighed,
before a single word was said.

He climbed the plinth one autumn night,
this radical who craved the light,
and tore the bandage from her eyes
to find not slumber, no disguise
of simple sleep or studied rest—
beneath the cloth, a cancer pressed
against her sockets, weeping sores
of old corruption, ancient wars
between the wealthy and the poor,
the owner and the laborer.

Her eyes were rotted, filled with rust,
the very organs we should trust
long since gone blind from what she'd seen
and chosen not to intervene:
the Pinkertons, the owners' gold,
the workingmen bought and sold,
the strike, the fear, the planted lie,
the men condemned who had to die
not for the bomb whose thrower's name
was never known, was never claimed—
but for the words they dared to say,
for organizing for a wage,
for eight-hour days, for dignity,
for daring to imagine free.

The boy stepped back, the bandage gone,
and morning came, and morning shone
upon a goddess who could see
at last her own hypocrisy—
not blind by choice, not blind by law,
but blind from refusing what she saw,
her disease now naked to the day:
the poor kept poor, the state's blood-pay,
the widows of the hanged men still
demanding answers, always will.

They buried Spies with open eyes,
his final words become our cries:
"There will be a time when our silence
is more powerful than the voices you strangle today."

And still she stands in marble cold,
her ancient wound still going untold
unless some radical, some youth,
dares climb again to unveil truth—
to strip the gauze, to make us see
that Justice, too, must learn to bleed
before she opens up her eyes
to hear the hanged men's final cries.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: In the style of Edgar Lee Masters, give me the epitaph of a Spoon River editor who was tarred and feathered for publishing an inflammatory allegory during a politically charged event.
counterfactuals.output:
**Thaddeus Kirkwood**

I wrote of the Wolf and the Fold,
Of the Serpent who wore the face of the Mayor,
And thought myself clever beyond the reach of the mob,
Hidden in fable, safe in the skin of a story.
They knew me anyway—
Every farmer and shopkeep in Spoon River
Could count the legs of my allegory
And find their own likeness beneath the fur.

They came at night with a bucket and a bag of feathers,
And I who had always loved the sound of my own words
Learned the language of silence,
Stripped and painted like a strange bird
Who would never fly again in Spoon River,
Nor print another line.

Village Wit, they called me after,
Not knowing that the tar sank deeper than my skin—
It sealed my mouth for good,
Long before the fever took me
Two winters on.

I tell you now, from this quiet plot:
The pen is not mightier than the mob
When the mob has read your paper
And found itself the villain of the piece.
Better to have written nothing
Than to have written truth
Dressed as a lie
That everyone could see through
Except the fool who penned it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a symbolic poem describing a blindfolded woman with a sword and scale dispensing arbitrary justice, ending with the crowd discovering the horror beneath her blindfold.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weighing

She stands upon the courthouse steps,
her arms grown tired from ancient weight—
in one hand, iron tongues of scale,
in one hand, sorrow's polished blade.

The cloth across her eyes is worn
so thin now, light seeps through the weave,
and yet she swears she cannot see
the ones who kneel, who beg, who grieve.

*Blind is fair,* the people say,
*for blindness cannot favor gold,
cannot see silk from beggar's rags,
cannot see young from bent and old.*

So they line up before her feet,
the guilty and the innocent both,
and cast their fates like dice or coin,
and she decides—by chance, by oath?

Her scale tips left. Her scale tips right.
A child taken for a debt.
A murderer walks free at dawn.
No pattern that the mind has met.

*She does not see, so she is just,*
they whisper, kneeling in the square,
while somewhere else a mother screams
at verdicts handed out like air.

The years wear on. The blade grows dull
from use on necks both foul and pure.
The scale hangs crooked, never fixed,
its balance nothing one can cure.

Then one day, wind, or rat, or time
unpicks the knot behind her head,
and slowly, slowly, does it fall—
that veil the people called their thread.

The crowd draws close. They mean to thank her,
to see the eyes that judged so true,
to find the wisdom in her gaze,
the fairness that they never knew.

But where her eyes should hold the world,
should hold some spark of thought or care,
there is no iris, white, or dark—
no orb at all. There's nothing there.

Just hollow sockets, black and deep,
two empty wells where sight should dwell.
She never chose. She never saw.
She simply—swung. She simply fell

into whatever shape the crowd
had carved for her with their own need,
a vessel for their want of order,
blind not by design, but greed—

for someone else to bear the weight
of every choice they feared to make.
The scale was never hers to hold.
The blindfold hid their own mistake.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
